title: States of matter
learningObjective: Understand the three states of matter in terms of the arrangement, movement and energy of the particles; Understand the interconversions between the three states of matter in terms of: the names of the interconversions; how they are achieved; the changes in arrangement, movement and energy of the particles; Know what is meant by the terms: solvent; solute; solution; saturated solution; CHEMISTRY ONLY — Know what is meant by the term solubility in the units g per 100 g of solvent; Understand how the results of experiments involving the dilution of coloured solutions and diffusion of gases can be explained

sections.title: States of matter — the particle idea
sections.markdown:
Everything around you — metals, concrete, water, the air you breathe, even
clouds — is made of **particles** that are far too small to see. That single
idea is called the [[particle-model]], and it is the key that unlocks the
whole of this chapter. In it we look at how the particles are arranged in
solids, liquids and gases, and at the ways the particles can move around.
What the particles themselves actually are (atoms, ions or molecules) is a
story for Chapter 3 — this chapter deliberately stays with the model, not
the particle types.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- describe the three states of matter in terms of the **arrangement,
  movement and energy** of their particles;
- understand the interconversions between the three states: their names,
  how they are achieved, and the changes in arrangement, movement and
  energy of the particles;
- define the terms **solvent**, **solute**, **solution** and **saturated
  solution**;
- *(Chemistry only)* define **solubility** in g per 100 g of solvent, plot
  and interpret solubility curves, and describe the solubility practical;
- explain how experiments on the **dilution** of coloured solutions and the
  **diffusion** of gases are evidence for the [[particle-model]].

:::key-point
The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. The [[particle-model]]
explains their properties in terms of the arrangement, separation and motion
of particles — and the [[kinetic-energy]] of those particles.
:::

:::prior-knowledge
Before this lesson you should be comfortable with **elements, compounds and
mixtures** vocabulary from Key Stage 3, and with reading simple particle
diagrams. This is the first chapter of Unit 1 — there is no earlier lesson
to link back to, so the Prior Knowledge you need is from KS3.
:::

:::cross-curricular
**Maths:** comparing the density of solids, liquids and gases is ratio and
proportion reasoning; the dilution estimate in §s10 uses powers of ten.
**Physics:** changes of state reappear in thermal-energy transfer — the
same [[particle-model]] vocabulary is used there.
:::

:::misconception
"Heating makes particles expand." No — when a solid is heated and melts, the
**spaces between** particles increase and the particles move faster; the
particles themselves do not get bigger.
:::

:::exam-hint
Command word **"State"** (1 mark): one short line, no explanation needed.
For "describe" questions, mark schemes accept answers in terms of
*arrangement, separation and motion* — e.g. "particles move faster" for
melting. Answers claiming particles "expand" score nothing.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: - spec 1.1 × 2 items (one "state", one "describe the
arrangement…"); - spec 1.1 × 1 item on comparing energies of the three
states.
:::

sections.title: The three states of matter
sections.markdown:
Solids, liquids and gases are known as **the three states of matter**. That
is the whole definition — but it is worth pausing on it, because it is
beautifully sweeping: everything you look at is a solid, a liquid or a gas. Water is our everyday demonstration substance: ice
(solid), tap water (liquid) and steam (gas) are the same substance existing
in all three states at different temperatures.

Which state a substance is in is not random — it is decided by how its
particles are arranged, how far apart they are, and how they move. That is
exactly what §s04 puts on the table, so if you want the full particle
pictures, read on and we will build them properly there.

:::key-point
The three states of matter are **solid, liquid and gas**. Every substance
you will meet is one of the three (or changing between two
of them).
:::

:::misconception
"Clouds are a special fourth state of matter — they are not solid, liquid
or gas." No — a cloud is made of tiny liquid water droplets suspended in
air (a gas mixture). Everything is one of the three states.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the three states of matter" (1 mark): list all three — solid,
liquid, gas — in any order. Mark schemes accept the three words alone; no
explanation is needed for a "State" command word.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.1 × 1 item ("state the three states of matter").
:::

sections.title: States of matter — facts around you
sections.markdown:
Try these three facts on for size — three everyday observations that the
particle model has to explain:

- You can't walk through a brick wall, but you *can* move — with some
  resistance, it pushes back against you — through water in a swimming
  pool. Moving through air is easy.
- When you melt most solids their volume increases slightly. Most liquids
  are less dense than the solid they come from.
- If you boil about 5 cm³ of water, the steam that comes off will fill an
  average bucket.

The [[particle-model]] explains all three at once. The particles in a solid
are held by strong forces of attraction and cannot move out of your way —
so the brick wall stops you. In a liquid the particles can be pushed aside
— so you can swim through water. In a gas there are (almost) no forces
between the particles, and they are far apart — so walking through air is
effortless. And when a solid melts, small gaps open up between the
particles, which is why most liquids are slightly less dense than their
solids; when a liquid boils, the particles separate hugely, which is why
5 cm³ of water makes a bucketful of steam.

:::key-point
- You can't walk through a brick wall because of the strong forces of
  attraction between the particles — they can't move out of your way.
- You can swim through water because you can push the particles out of
  the way.
- It is easy to move through a gas because there are (almost) no forces
  between the particles.
:::

:::did-you-know
5 cm³ of water becomes enough steam to fill an average bucket. That is how
much further apart gas particles are compared with particles in a liquid.
:::

:::misconception
"You can walk through air because air has no particles." No — air is full
of gas particles; you pass through easily because they are far apart and
there are (almost) no forces between them, not because they are absent.
:::

:::exam-hint
When you draw particle diagrams: in a solid the particles are close
together and usually regularly packed; in a liquid make sure the particles
are **mostly touching** their neighbours (the packing need not be regular
— what matters is close together with some gaps).
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.1 × 2 items — one on
explaining "why can you walk through air but not a wall" in particle terms,
one on particle diagrams for the three states.
:::

sections.title: Particles in solids, liquids and gases
sections.markdown:
Here are the particle pictures for all three states, with the exact
descriptions to memorise. In a
**solid**, the particles are usually arranged regularly and packed closely
together. They can only vibrate about fixed positions — they cannot move
around — because strong forces of attraction hold them together.

In a **liquid**, the particles are still mostly touching, but some gaps
have appeared between them. This is why liquids are usually less dense
than the solids they come from. The forces between the particles are less
effective, so the particles can move around each other; the arrangement is
random rather than regular.

In a **gas**, the particles are much further apart and there are (almost)
no forces of attraction between them. They move randomly at high speed in
all directions. The energy story runs in the same order: the particles in
a solid have less [[kinetic-energy]] than the particles in a liquid, which
have less [[kinetic-energy]] than the particles in a gas.

:::key-point
Learn the three-part description for each state — **arrangement**
(regular/random), **separation** (touching / touching with gaps / far
apart) and **motion** (vibrate about fixed positions / move around each
other / move randomly at high speed) — plus the energy ordering
solid < liquid < gas.
:::

:::misconception
"There are no forces at all between gas particles." Almost — *almost* no
forces. Very weak attractions do exist; they are what let a
gas condense to a liquid when it is cooled enough.
:::

:::exam-hint
A 6-mark "compare the particles in solids and liquids" answer scores by
covering arrangement, separation, motion and energy. Mark schemes accept
phrases like "vibrate about fixed positions", "move around each other" and
"move randomly and fast". "Particles in a liquid are freer" alone is too
vague to score.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.1 × 2 items — draw/describe
the three particle arrangements; compare kinetic energies. spec 1.2 × 1
item linking gaps to density on melting.
:::

sections.title: Melting, freezing, boiling and condensing
sections.markdown:
Heat a solid and the energy from the heat source makes its particles
vibrate faster and faster. Eventually they vibrate so fast that the forces
of attraction are no longer strong enough to hold them together — the
particles can move around each other, and the solid **[[melting]]s** into
a liquid. The temperature at which this happens is the **[[melting-point]]**. Energy has to be supplied to get
there, because the liquid particles end up with more [[kinetic-energy]]
than the solid particles had.

Cool the liquid again and its particles move more and more slowly, until
the forces of attraction can hold them in fixed positions — packing more
closely together into a solid. The liquid **[[freezing]]s**. The
temperature at which this happens is the freezing point — and although the
two directions have different names, the melting point and the freezing
point of a substance are **exactly the same temperature**.

Boiling is the liquid-to-gas change that happens when a liquid is heated
so strongly that particles move fast enough to overcome **all** the forces
of attraction between them. The stronger those forces are, the higher the
**[[boiling-point]]** — more energy is needed to beat them. Cool a gas and
its particles eventually slow enough for attractions to form and hold
them together as a liquid: the gas **[[condensation]]s**.

One warning before you leave this section: evaporation is *not* boiling.
Evaporation occurs at **any** temperature; boiling occurs only at the
[[boiling-point]]. UK puddles disappear in winter at
temperatures well below 5 °C — the water certainly is not boiling; it is
evaporating. Water evaporates at, say, 5 °C but boils only at 100 °C.

:::key-point
Melting point = freezing point (same temperature, different direction).
Boiling happens only at the boiling point; evaporation happens at any
temperature.
:::

:::misconception
"A liquid must reach its boiling point before any of it can turn into a
gas." No — evaporation happens at any temperature from the surface;
boiling is the special, faster change that occurs throughout the liquid at
one temperature.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Name the change of state" questions (1 mark each): solid→liquid =
melting; liquid→solid = freezing; liquid→gas = boiling *or* evaporation;
gas→liquid = condensing. Mark schemes accept both spellings/gerunds
("condensation"/"condensing").
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.2 × 3 items — name the four
interconversions; explain why melting point and freezing point coincide;
contrast evaporation and boiling in particle terms.
:::

sections.title: Evaporation — and sublimation
sections.markdown:
[[evaporation]] is different from boiling, and the difference is all in the
particles. In any liquid, the *average* speed of the particles varies with
temperature — but at each temperature some particles are moving faster
than the average and others more slowly. Some very fast particles at the
**surface** of the liquid have enough [[kinetic-energy]] to overcome the
forces of attraction between particles: they break away and form a gas.
That is evaporation. You see no bubbling — an open liquid just slowly
disappears.

In a **closed container** the story gains a second half. Gas particles
collide with particles at the liquid surface; those moving slowly enough
are held by the attractive forces and rejoin the liquid. So in a closed
container evaporation and [[condensation]] are both occurring at the same
time.

Some substances skip the liquid stage entirely. A small number can change
directly from solid to gas — or gas to solid — at normal pressure. Solid
to gas is **[[sublimation]]**; gas to solid is usually called
**[[deposition]]**. Dry ice — solid carbon dioxide — subliming in a
beaker makes the point vividly: the white cloud is *not* carbon dioxide (which is
an invisible gas); it forms because the CO₂ gas is so cold that it makes
water vapour in the air condense.

Finally, a definitions note you will use in §s08: in science,
**[[room-temperature]]** usually means between 20 and 25 °C. There is not
one fixed value, so when a change of state happens near room temperature,
always make clear which value you are using.

:::key-point
Sublimation = solid → gas directly. Deposition = gas → solid directly.
Both happen without a liquid forming, at normal pressure.
:::

:::did-you-know
The white cloud over dry ice is condensed water vapour from the air, not
the carbon dioxide itself — CO₂ gas is invisible.
:::

:::misconception
"The white cloud around dry ice is carbon dioxide gas." No — carbon
dioxide gas is invisible. The cloud is water vapour from the air
condensing because the CO₂ gas is so cold.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why a puddle can disappear even when the temperature is below
5 °C." Mark schemes accept: *some particles (at the surface) move faster
than average / have enough energy to overcome the forces of attraction and
escape from the liquid*. Avoid answers that claim the puddle boils.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.2 × 3 items — evaporation
vs boiling; closed-container evaporation + condensation; naming
sublimation/deposition.
:::

sections.title: Dry ice and carbon dioxide's states
sections.markdown:
Carbon dioxide is the poster child for [[sublimation]]. At ordinary
pressures there is **no such thing as liquid carbon dioxide** — the solid
turns directly into a gas at **−78.5 °C**, well below [[room-temperature]].
Solid carbon dioxide is known as **dry ice**, and it doubles as a handy
source of gas particles: let an ammonia particle bounce off air particles
and you have a hint of what diffusion is all about, which is where we go
next (§s09).

This section is short by design: a dry-ice story that closes out the
changes of state before the move into diffusion. Master it, then follow us
into diffusion.

:::key-point
At ordinary pressures carbon dioxide sublimes at −78.5 °C — solid dry ice
becomes gas with no liquid in between.
:::

:::misconception
"Dry ice melts into liquid carbon dioxide, like ordinary ice melts into
water." No — at ordinary pressures liquid CO₂ does not exist; the solid
sublimes straight to gas at −78.5 °C.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the physical state of carbon dioxide at −80 °C / at room
temperature." At −80 °C (below −78.5 °C) it is solid; at room temperature
it is gas. Mark schemes want the state only — but be ready to explain
using melting/sublimation temperatures in a second part.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.2 × 2 items — sublimation
temperature of CO₂; state of CO₂ at a given temperature.
:::

sections.title: Predicting state from melting and boiling points
sections.markdown:
Here is the rule that turns melting and boiling points into a prediction
machine. A substance is:

- a **solid** at temperatures **below its [[melting-point]]**;
- a **liquid** **between its melting point and its [[boiling-point]]**;
- a **gas** **above its boiling point**.

To decide the state at room temperature, use [[room-temperature]] (20–25
°C) and place the two fixed points on a temperature line. Oxygen's
boiling point sits *below* room
temperature, so oxygen is a gas at room temperature. Lithium's melting
point sits *above* room temperature, so lithium is a solid. Bromine, as
the worked example below shows, is a liquid.

:::worked-example
**Bromine from −100 °C to 100 °C** (melting point −7 °C, boiling point 59
°C):

1. At −100 °C — below bromine's melting point — bromine is a **solid**.
2. Heated to −7 °C it **melts**; from −7 °C to 59 °C it remains a
   **liquid**.
3. Room temperature (20–25 °C) falls inside that liquid range, so bromine
   is a **liquid at room temperature**.
4. Above 59 °C bromine is a **gas**.
:::

:::key-point
Below the melting point → solid. Between melting point and boiling point →
liquid. Above the boiling point → gas. The state at room temperature is
decided entirely by where room temperature sits relative to the two fixed
points.
:::

:::misconception
"Anything liquid at room temperature must have a low boiling point." No —
bromine's boiling point is 59 °C, which is not low, yet bromine is liquid
at 20–25 °C because room temperature is above its melting point *and*
below its boiling point.
:::

:::maths-skills
Draw a horizontal temperature line, mark room temperature on it, then plot
the melting and boiling points of the substance. Where the points land
relative to the room-temperature mark gives the state — this is the
fastest reliable exam technique for these questions.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why bromine is a liquid at room temperature" (2 marks): state
that room temperature is **above bromine's melting point** and **below its
boiling point**. Mark schemes accept "melting point below room temperature
/ boiling point above room temperature" — always quote the values you are
using for room temperature.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.2 × 2 items — predict state
at a stated temperature; explain state at room temperature from mp/bp.
:::

sections.title: Diffusion
sections.markdown:
Someone releases a smelly gas — ammonia, say — at the front of the lab.
Within a minute or so everybody can smell it. That is not surprising:
particles in a gas are free to move around.
What needs explaining is why it takes **so long**. At room temperature
ammonia particles travel at about **600 metres per second**, so travelling
in straight lines they would cross the lab in under 0.01 s. Instead, each
particle is bouncing off air particles on the way — by the time the smell
reaches every corner, an ammonia particle may have travelled **30 or more
kilometres**.

That spreading out is **[[diffusion]]**: the movement of particles from
where they are at a **high [[concentration]]** (lots of them in a certain
volume) to where they are at a **low concentration** (fewer in that
volume), ending with particles spread out evenly.

Two classic experiments demonstrate diffusion:

1. **Bromine and air**: a lower gas jar holds brown bromine
   gas; the upper jar holds air. Remove the lids and the brown colour
   diffuses upwards until *both* jars are uniformly brown — air particles
   diffuse downwards at the same time. Random movement gives an even
   mixture of both gases everywhere.
2. **Hydrogen and air**: same experiment, but you must lower a lighted
   splint in at the end to find where the hydrogen went. People expect the
   much less dense hydrogen to end up only in the top jar — in fact you
   get **identical explosions from both jars**.

**Different gases diffuse at different speeds.** The classic evidence: a
long glass tube with cotton wool soaked in concentrated ammonia solution
at one end and concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other. Ammonia and
hydrogen chloride gases diffuse along the tube and react where they meet:
NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s) — a **white ring** of solid ammonium chloride.
The ring takes minutes to form (diffusion takes time) and forms **closer
to the hydrochloric acid end**, because ammonia particles (relative
molecular mass 17) are **lighter** than hydrogen chloride particles (36.5)
and therefore move faster, travelling further in the same time.

:::safety
These are **teacher demonstrations only**. The bromine and
ammonia/hydrogen chloride demos must be prepared in a working fume
cupboard with eye protection and chemical-resistant gloves; bromine
inhalation can cause delayed reactions needing urgent medical attention.
Skin contact and fume inhalation must be avoided; clean-up happens in the
fume cupboard. (You will learn about relative molecular mass properly in
Chapter 5.)
:::

:::key-point
Diffusion = spreading out of particles from high concentration to low
concentration. Lighter particles (lower relative molecular mass) diffuse
faster.
:::

:::misconception
"With hydrogen in the bottom jar, only the top jar would explode —
hydrogen rises because it is light." No — after the lids are removed both
gases diffuse into both jars, so the experiment gives identical explosions
in *both* jars.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Explain why the white ring forms nearer the hydrochloric acid end" (2–3
marks): ammonia particles are **lighter** (smaller relative molecular
mass) so they move **faster** and travel **further in the same time**.
Mark schemes accept "lighter/smaller mass particles move faster"; avoid
teleology like "ammonia wants to travel further".
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.3 × 4 items — define
diffusion; explain the bromine jar result; the NH₃/HCl ring position;
predict the ring position with HBr.
:::

sections.title: Diffusion in liquids — and how tiny particles are
sections.markdown:
[[diffusion]] through a **liquid** is very slow if the liquid is
completely still. Place a small jar of strongly coloured potassium
manganate(VII) solution in a gas jar of water and it can take **days** for
the colour to spread through all the water. Two reasons, straight from the
[[particle-model]]: particles in a liquid move more slowly than particles
in a gas, and they are much closer together — so there is less space to
move into without colliding with another particle.

This coloured solution then powers one of the most beautiful estimates in
the whole course — estimating an upper limit on the mass of a single
particle:

1. Dissolve **0.01 g** of potassium manganate(VII) in **1 cm³** of water —
   a deep purple [[solution]].
2. One drop is about **0.05 cm³**, so there are **20 drops** in 1 cm³, and
   each drop contains 0.0005 g.
3. Dilute the solution until the total volume is **10 000 cm³** — the
   colour is *still just visible*. There are now **200 000 drops**, and
   for each drop to look purple, each drop must contain **at least one
   'particle'**.
4. So at least 200 000 'particles' must fit in 0.01 g — each 'particle'
   can weigh no more than **5 × 10⁻⁸ g** (0.00000005 g).

That estimate is *not even close* to the real answer — a potassium
manganate(VII) 'particle' actually weighs about **2.6 × 10⁻²² g**, and
there are about **38 000 000 000 000 000 000** particles in 0.01 g. In
reality you need enormous numbers of particles in each drop for the colour
to register. Dilution does not remove particles — it only spreads them
further apart.

Why the inverted commas around 'particle'? Potassium manganate(VII) is an
**ionic compound**, so it contains more than one sort of particle — you
will find out what that means in Chapter 7.

:::key-point
Diffusion in a still liquid is slow because liquid particles move slowly
and are close together. The visibility of a dilute colour proves that a
tiny mass contains an enormous number of particles.
:::

:::misconception
"Diluting a solution removes some of the particles." No — dilution only
spreads the same particles through a larger volume; the total number of
particles is unchanged, which is exactly why the colour survives such huge
dilution.
:::

:::maths-skills
Standard form is the honest language for this section: 5 × 10⁻⁸ g upper
limit, 2.6 × 10⁻²² g actual, 3.8 × 10¹⁹ particles. Chain the estimate one
step at a time (mass per drop → number of drops → particles per drop) and
each step is easy.
:::

:::did-you-know
In 0.01 g of potassium manganate(VII) there are about
38 000 000 000 000 000 000 particles — roughly 38 quintillion. You need
very large numbers of particles in each drop for your eye to see the
colour at all.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Suggest what this experiment tells us about the size of particles" (2
marks): the particles must be **extremely small** — a very large number of
them fit into a tiny mass. Mark schemes accept "particles are very small";
avoid "particles are invisible" (no evidence) or "particles disappear".
:::

:::cross-curricular
**Maths:** powers of ten and estimation — this section is a worked lesson
in Fermi-estimate reasoning (upper bounds from visible evidence).
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.3 × 3 items — why liquid
diffusion is slow; the dilution-estimate logic; what the estimate proves
about particle size.
:::

sections.title: Solute, solvent, solution — and measuring solubility
sections.markdown:
When a solid dissolves in a liquid, the vocabulary is fixed: the substance
that dissolves is the **[[solute]]**; the liquid it dissolves in is the
**[[solvent]]**; the liquid formed is a **[[solution]]**. At the particle
level, dissolving means the attractive forces between the particles in the
solute are broken, while new attractive forces form between solvent
particles and solute particles. Whether a particular solid is soluble in a
particular solvent depends on whether the new forces are strong enough to
overcome the old ones.

Only a certain amount of solute will dissolve in a fixed amount of
solvent at a particular temperature. When that maximum is dissolved —
with some undissolved solid still present — you have a **[[saturated-solution]]**. Keep some undissolved solid there: it
prevents supersaturated solutions forming (an extension idea you do not
need at International GCSE).

> **CHEMISTRY ONLY** — everything from here to the end of §s13 is
> Paper 2 content (spec points 1.5C, 1.6C, 1.7C).

The **[[solubility]]** of a solid in a solvent at a particular temperature
is defined as *the mass of solute which must dissolve in 100 g of solvent
at that temperature to form a saturated solution*. For example, the
solubility of sodium chloride in water at 25 °C is about **36 g per 100 g
of water**.

**Practical: measuring the solubility of potassium nitrate at 40 °C.**
Weigh an evaporating basin; heat water in a boiling tube to just above 40
°C; add potassium nitrate stirring rapidly until no more dissolves (some
solid left over); allow the solution to cool to exactly 40 °C; pour off
some solution into the basin — **solution only, no solid**; weigh basin +
contents; heat gently to evaporate off the water; re-weigh, then heat and
re-weigh again — **heating to constant mass** — to be sure all the water
has gone. With a recorded set of results (basin 25.72 g; basin +
solution 58.00 g; basin + dry crystals 38.00 g): mass of solid = 12.28 g,
mass of water
= 20.00 g. Twelve point two eight grams dissolves in 20.00 g of water, so
five times as much dissolves in 100 g — the solubility of potassium
nitrate at 40 °C is **61.4 g per 100 g of water**. In general:
**solubility (g per 100 g) = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solvent) × 100**.

:::key-point
A saturated solution contains the maximum mass of dissolved solid at that
temperature, with undissolved solid present. Solubility is always quoted
**with a temperature**: "the solubility of sodium chloride at 30 °C is…".
:::

:::maths-skills
From the balance readings: solid = 38.00 − 25.72 = 12.28 g; water =
58.00 − 38.00 = 20.00 g; scale to 100 g: 12.28 × (100 ÷ 20.00) = 61.4 g
per 100 g. Learn the scaling equation — it appears in exam data questions
constantly.
:::

:::misconception
"Solubility is a fixed property — the same value at any temperature." No —
solubility varies with temperature, which is why a temperature must
always be quoted alongside the value.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Why is the solution heated gently?" — so none of it spits out; spitting
would lose solid and give a solubility reading **lower** than the true
value. "Why heat to constant mass?" — to confirm all the water has
evaporated. Mark schemes accept "mass no longer changes / all water
removed".
:::

:::safety
Wear eye protection and heat gently — hot solid can spit out of the
evaporating basin and cause burns.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.4 × 2 (solute/solvent/
solution/saturated definitions); spec 1.5C × 1 (define solubility, quote
temperature); spec 1.7C × 2 (practical method + constant-mass reasoning).
:::

sections.title: Solubility curves
sections.markdown:
**CHEMISTRY ONLY.** Solubility changes with temperature, so plot
[[solubility]] against temperature and you get a **solubility curve**.
Most solids have curves like those for potassium nitrate and potassium
chloride: solubility **increases** with
temperature — either dramatically (KNO₃) or only a little (KCl).

Solubility curves earn their keep by predicting **crystals**. Take
potassium nitrate: at 90 °C, 200 g dissolves in 100 g of water; at 30 °C
only 50 g will dissolve. So a solution containing 200 g of potassium
nitrate in 100 g of water, cooled from 90 °C to 30 °C, must release
200 − 50 = **150 g** of solid. We say the potassium nitrate
**[[crystallisation]]s out** of the solution — or precipitates out — as
crystals.

One graph-drawing note: the solubility curve here is
virtually a straight line, but that will not always be the case — if you
are asked to draw a line of best fit, it can be either a straight line or
a curve.

:::key-point
Mass of crystals formed on cooling = difference between the solubility
values at the starting and finishing temperatures (for the same mass of
solvent).
:::

:::maths-skills
Cooling a saturated solution: crystals = solubility(hot) − solubility(cool),
scaled to however much solvent you actually have (see §s13 for the scaling
method).
:::

:::misconception
"Cooling a saturated solution makes more solute dissolve." No — cooling
lowers the solubility of most solids, so the excess solute comes **out**
of the solution as crystals.
:::

:::exam-hint
Read the axes before anything else — temperature on the horizontal axis,
solubility (g per 100 g of water) on the vertical. Use dashed construction
lines to read values; mark schemes allow small read-off tolerances.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 1.6C × 2 items — read a
value off a solubility curve; calculate mass of crystals on cooling.
:::

sections.title: Worked example — reading a solubility curve
sections.markdown:
**CHEMISTRY ONLY.** This worked example uses potassium chloride, with
solubilities measured at five temperatures:

| Temperature/°C | 10 | 30 | 40 | 70 | 90 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Solubility/g per 100 g of water | 31.2 | 37.2 | 40.0 | 48.5 | 53.9 |

**(a) Plot the curve.** Temperature on the horizontal axis, solubility on
the vertical one; plot the five points and join them smoothly (Figure
1.19).

**(b)(i) Solubility at 50 °C.** Reading the curve at 50 °C gives **42.5 g
per 100 g of water**.

**(b)(ii) Maximum mass dissolving in 50 g of water at 40 °C.** The curve
gives 40 g per 100 g at 40 °C — so half the mass of water dissolves half
the mass: **20 g** in 50 g of water. For any other mass of water, scale
with the equation: mass dissolved = (mass of water ÷ 100) × solubility.
For instance, in 34.6 g of water at 40 °C: (34.6 ÷ 100) × 40 =
**13.84 g** of potassium chloride dissolves.

**(b)(iii) When do crystals first appear?** A hot solution contains 51.0 g
of potassium chloride in 100 g of water, and is left to cool. Crystals
appear as soon as the solution becomes saturated — that is, when 51.0 g
is the maximum that can stay dissolved. Drawing a line across at 51.0 g
shows this happens at **80 °C**: below that temperature the solution is
saturated and crystals form. (In different circumstances you might need to
read the 10 °C value from the graph as well — for example, cooling to
10 °C leaves 31.2 g dissolved, so 51.0 − 31.2 = 19.8 g of crystals form.)

This lesson's practice is wired to the question bank below.

:::worked-example
The three readings above — 42.5 g per 100 g at 50 °C; 20 g in 50 g of
water at 40 °C; crystals first below 80 °C for a 51.0 g solution — are
the full exam skill set: **read the curve, scale to the solvent mass,
find the saturation temperature.**
:::

:::maths-skills
The scaling equation mass = (mass of water ÷ 100) × solubility works in
both directions: given the water mass it predicts the dissolved mass;
given the dissolved mass (51.0 g) it pins the temperature at which
crystals first appear.
:::

:::misconception
"A solubility curve is always a straight line." No — the potassium
chloride curve here is virtually straight, but most curves bend (potassium
nitrate's rises steeply). A line of best fit can be a curve.
:::

:::exam-hint
Graph questions: draw dashed construction lines from the axis to the
curve and quote values to the precision the grid allows. Mark schemes
accept read-off tolerance — but a missing temperature or unit ("per 100 g
of water") loses marks.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.6C × 3 items — read solubility at a temperature;
scale to a non-100 g solvent mass; find the crystallisation temperature.
:::

:::summary
- Matter is solid, liquid or gas; the [[particle-model]] explains states
  by particle arrangement, separation, motion and energy.
- Interconversions: melting/freezing (solid↔liquid), boiling/condensing
  (liquid↔gas), evaporation (any temperature), sublimation/deposition
  (solid↔gas directly).
- State at a temperature = where that temperature sits relative to the
  melting and boiling points (room temperature = 20–25 °C).
- Diffusion = spreading from high to low concentration; lighter particles
  diffuse faster; liquids diffuse slowly.
- Solute + solvent = solution; a saturated solution holds the maximum
  dissolved solid at that temperature; solubility is quoted in g per 100 g
  of solvent **with a temperature** (Chemistry only, with curves and the
  practical).
:::

:::can-you
- [ ] describe each state in terms of arrangement, separation and motion?
- [ ] name all the interconversions and say how each is achieved?
- [ ] predict the state of a substance at any temperature from its
      melting and boiling points?
- [ ] explain the ammonia/hydrogen chloride white-ring experiment,
      including why the ring forms nearer one end?
- [ ] define solute, solvent, solution and saturated solution?
- [ ] *(C)* calculate a solubility in g per 100 g from experiment data?
- [ ] *(C)* read a solubility curve to find dissolved mass, crystal mass
      and saturation temperature?
:::
